13830: To revel means to take intense, open, and enthusiastic pleasure in something — or to celebrate in a loud, joyful, festive way. It's not quiet or subtle enjoyment. When someone revels, they are fully soaking themselves in the experience, often showing it openly and without restraint.

Meaning 1: To revel in something — to deeply and enthusiastically enjoy or take pleasure in something.

This is the most common use. The structure is almost always revel + in. Think of it as the difference between enjoying a warm bath and melting into a warm bath. Reveling is the second one — immersive, whole-hearted, and often visible to others.

Examples:

  • She reveled in the applause after her performance. (She didn't just appreciate the clapping — she soaked up every second of it, openly and joyfully.)
  • He reveled in the attention his new car attracted.
  • The children reveled in the freedom of summer vacation.
  • After years of hard work, she finally got to revel in her success.

Meaning 2: To revel (without "in") — to celebrate in a lively, noisy, and joyful way; to party with great energy and enthusiasm.

This sense is about festive, exuberant celebration — think dancing in the streets, loud laughter, feasting, merriment.

Examples:

  • Fans reveled in the streets after their team won the championship.
  • They reveled until dawn after the wedding.
  • The whole town reveled when the war ended.

Note that these two meanings often overlap. "Fans reveled in the streets" captures both the festive celebration AND the deep joy they felt. That's why the word is so expressive — it can carry both senses at once.

Revel in something — This is the go-to pattern for Meaning 1.

  • She revels in the chaos. (present)
  • He reveled in being the center of attention. (past)
  • They were reveling in their victory. (ongoing action)

For Meaning 2, you often see it used without "in":

  • They reveled all night long.
  • The crowd reveled for hours.

Revel carries a strong sense of indulgence and active participation in pleasure. It is not passive. When you revel in something, you are not just sitting back and mildly appreciating it — you are leaning into it, drinking it in, savoring it with your whole self.

There is also a sense of freedom in the word. To revel often implies letting go of restraint. That's why the word feels joyful and alive — it suggests someone who is not holding back.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Enjoy — General and neutral. You can enjoy a quiet cup of tea. Revel is far more intense and expressive. You wouldn't say "she reveled in her cup of tea" unless she was making a big moment out of it.

Delight in — Very close to revel in, but more refined and gentle. "She delighted in the music" feels elegant and calm. "She reveled in the music" feels more immersive and energetic.

Bask in — Also similar. To bask is to soak in something pleasant passively, like a cat lying in sunlight. It's warm but still. To revel is more active — there's energy and enthusiasm in it.

Celebrate — Relates to Meaning 2, but celebrate is broad and neutral. Reveling implies a particularly lively, unrestrained kind of celebration, not just a formal acknowledgment.
When Revel Has a Slightly Negative Shade

Because reveling implies enthusiastic, uninhibited pleasure, it can take on a negative tone when someone enjoys something that others find inappropriate or unsettling.

  • He seemed to revel in other people's failures. (This suggests he took a disturbing, excessive pleasure in watching others fail — almost gloating.)
  • She reveled in the drama, stirring up conflict at every chance.

In these cases, the word highlights that the enjoyment goes beyond what's considered decent. The same quality that makes revel feel joyful in positive contexts — its intensity and lack of restraint — is exactly what makes it feel uncomfortable in negative ones.

Think of revel as the word you reach for when ordinary enjoyment isn't strong enough. It signals full, enthusiastic, unashamed immersion in pleasure or celebration. Whether someone is reveling in a moment of personal triumph, or reveling at a festival with dancing and laughter, the word always tells you: this person is not holding back. They are giving themselves over entirely to the joy of the moment.
13831:
A revelation is the act of making something known that was hidden, secret, or unknown before — or it is the piece of information itself that gets uncovered. Think of it like lifting a curtain. Whatever was behind that curtain was always there, but now, for the first time, it is visible to someone.

The word works in two closely related ways:

  • The act of revealing: "The revelation of his true identity shocked everyone." (Here, revelation = the act of uncovering.)
  • The thing revealed: "The document contained several startling revelations." (Here, revelations = the actual pieces of information uncovered.)

Both uses are correct and extremely common.
The Two Big Flavors of Meaning

1. Everyday Meaning — A Surprising Discovery or Disclosure

In everyday life, a revelation is something you learn that you did not know before, and crucially, it changes the way you see things. It carries a strong sense of surprise, even shock. It is not just new information — it is information that feels significant, eye-opening, or transformative.

For example:

  • If you find out that your quiet neighbor used to be a spy, that is a revelation.
  • If a celebrity's private diary is published and exposes their secret struggles, those are revelations.
  • If a scientist announces a groundbreaking finding that overturns what everyone believed, that announcement is a revelation.

Notice the pattern: a revelation is not just any new fact. It is a fact that matters, that surprises, and that shifts your understanding in some meaningful way. It often comes with a feeling of "I never would have guessed this" or "this changes everything."

A revelation can also be something purely personal and internal — a moment of sudden, clear understanding. For example: "Reading that book was a revelation for me — I finally understood why I had been feeling lost." Here, nobody told you a secret; instead, something clicked inside your own mind. An insight arrived suddenly and clearly, like a light turning on in a dark room.

2. Religious and Spiritual Meaning — Divine Disclosure

In a religious context, especially in Christianity and other Abrahamic faiths, revelation refers to something that God (or a divine power) discloses to human beings. It is the idea that certain truths about God, the universe, or how humans should live cannot be figured out by ordinary human thinking — they can only be known because God chooses to reveal them.

So when theologians say "divine revelation," they mean: God making himself, his nature, or his will known to people. This can happen through sacred scriptures, prophets, visions, or direct spiritual experience.

This meaning is serious, formal, and carries enormous weight in religious traditions. It implies that the source of the information is not human at all — it comes from something far beyond ordinary life.
"Revelation" as a Proper Noun — The Book

When written with a capital R and used as a title — Revelation (or sometimes The Book of Revelation) — it refers to the last book of the Christian Bible. It is a prophetic and visionary text attributed to a figure named John, filled with symbolic imagery about the end of the world, judgment, and ultimate divine victory. It is also sometimes called The Apocalypse (a Greek word that literally means "uncovering" or "disclosure"). This is directly connected to the religious meaning above — the book presents itself as a divine unveiling of things to come.
What Makes "Revelation" Different from Similar Words

It helps to know how revelation differs from words that seem similar:

  • Discovery — You find something through your own effort, exploration, or accident. A scientist discovers a new species. The emphasis is on your active role. A revelation, by contrast, often lands on you — it is uncovered or disclosed, sometimes by someone else or by circumstances, often with a sense of surprise.
  • Disclosure — This is a more neutral, formal word. It simply means making information known (often used in legal or official contexts: "financial disclosure"). It carries no strong sense of surprise or significance. A revelation always feels significant; a disclosure might not.
  • Surprise — A surprise can be trivial (you didn't expect the pizza to arrive so fast). A revelation always carries weight and meaning. Every revelation is surprising, but not every surprise is a revelation.
  • Realization — This is a personal, internal moment of understanding — something clicks in your own mind. A revelation can mean this too (especially in informal use), but revelation more commonly involves information coming from outside you, while realization is generated within you.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Revelation" is not a neutral word. It almost always carries emotional force. When you use it, you are signaling that what was uncovered is significant, unexpected, and changes things. Because of this, people use it to emphasize impact. Writers, journalists, and speakers reach for this word when they want to convey that a piece of information was not merely new — it was stunning or transformative.

If you say "I had a revelation today," people immediately understand that something important happened to you mentally or emotionally — not that you simply learned a random fact.

SituationWhat "revelation" means

To pull it all together: a revelation is a disclosure of something that was hidden or unknown, typically one that is striking and meaningful. It can be the act of uncovering something or the thing uncovered itself. In everyday life it means a surprising, significant piece of information or a sudden eye-opening insight. In a religious context it means truth disclosed by God to humans. And as a proper noun, it is the final book of the Christian Bible. The common thread across all these meanings is the unveiling of something that was not visible before — and the sense that once revealed, things are never quite the same.
13832:
Revelry means loud, lively, joyful celebration — the kind where a group of people is having an uproariously good time together, often with music, dancing, laughter, and usually drinks. It's not just being happy; it's being boisterously, freely, exuberantly happy in a group setting.

Think of a street full of people celebrating a festival at midnight — shouting, laughing, dancing, clinking glasses. That is revelry.
What makes revelry different from just "fun" or "celebration"

The word carries three important qualities that ordinary words like "party" or "fun" don't fully capture:

  1. Noise and energy. Revelry is never quiet. It implies sounds — laughter, music, cheering, clinking. A calm, candle-lit dinner among friends is not revelry.
  2. A sense of letting go. People in revelry have dropped their inhibitions. They're not being careful or restrained. There's an element of abandon — of people giving themselves over completely to the joy of the moment.
  3. A group energy. Revelry is almost always collective. One person alone can't truly have revelry; it feeds off the energy of many people together.

Revelry is associated with occasions like:

  • New Year's Eve celebrations
  • Festival nights (Holi, Diwali, Mardi Gras, Carnival)
  • Victory celebrations after a war, a sports championship, or an election
  • Weddings and feast days
  • Any night where a crowd decides to celebrate with full force

It very commonly involves alcohol, though not always. It almost always involves music, dancing, or both.
The tone of the word — positive, but with a subtle edge

Revelry is mostly a positive word, but it carries a slight undertone of excess. It suggests celebration that is wild and unrestrained, perhaps going on longer than it should, perhaps getting louder than expected.

When a writer uses the word "revelry," they're painting a picture that is vivid, energetic, and slightly larger-than-life. It's a richer, more evocative word than "celebration" — it doesn't just tell you people are happy, it makes you feel the noise and energy of the scene.

Depending on who is speaking, it can be used admiringly ("the streets were filled with joyous revelry") or with mild disapproval ("the revelry kept the neighbors awake all night"). The word itself is neutral, but context decides which way it tips.

• The sounds of revelry drifted from the festival grounds late into the night.
  • After the team's victory, revelry erupted across the entire city.
  • The holiday revelry in the town square lasted until well past midnight.
  • He watched the revelry from his window, too tired to join but smiling at the sight.
  • The wedding was not an elegant affair — it was pure, unabashed revelry.

To sharpen your understanding, here's what the word does not describe:

  • A quiet, intimate gathering → not revelry
  • One person enjoying themselves alone → not revelry
  • A solemn ceremony or ritual, even a joyful one → not revelry
  • Polite applause or restrained happiness → not revelry

Revelry requires volume, energy, freedom, and company.

The plural form "revelries" is used when referring to multiple separate occasions or episodes of celebration.

  • The carnival's nightly revelries drew thousands of visitors.
  • The revelries of that summer are still talked about in the village.

• Revel (verb): to revel means to take part in revelry, or more broadly, to take great and obvious delight in something. "She reveled in the attention." / "They reveled all night."
  • Revel (noun, somewhat old-fashioned): a revel is an occasion of revelry — a wild, festive celebration. "The midnight revel drew crowds from across town."
  • Reveler (also spelled reveller): a person who is taking part in revelry. "The revelers danced in the streets until sunrise."
The feel of the word in writing

"Revelry" has a slightly literary, classical quality to it. You'll find it often in literature, news writing, and formal or expressive prose. It's not a word people use in casual everyday speech much ("there was so much revelry last night!"), but it's completely natural and appropriate in writing, storytelling, and descriptive language. When you use it, it elevates the sentence and adds a vivid, almost cinematic quality to the scene you're describing.
13833:
A revenant is a dead person — or sometimes a dead creature — who has come back from death and now exists among the living. The single most important thing to understand about this word is that the "coming back" is the whole point. A revenant is not just any ghost or spirit. It is specifically defined by the act of returning — crossing back over the line between death and life, and showing up again in the world of the living.

Think of it this way: imagine someone dies. They are gone. Then, somehow — they are back. That is a revenant.

In traditional folklore, a revenant is not a peaceful, faded, see-through ghost who quietly floats through walls. It is something far more unsettling. A revenant tends to be physical and present — more like a walking corpse than a wisp of light. It may look like the dead person it once was, but decayed, wrong, and disturbing. It can sometimes be touched, heard, and even smelled.

This physicality is what separates a revenant from a typical ghost in folklore. A ghost is often just a soul or an energy. A revenant is more of a body that came back — and that makes it far more threatening.

This is where it gets rich. In old folk stories and legends — particularly from medieval Europe — a revenant almost never came back without a reason. Common reasons include:

Revenge. The person was wronged, murdered, or treated unjustly in life, and they have come back to settle the score with whoever harmed them. They will not rest until justice (by their own definition) is done.

Unfinished business. Something was left incomplete — a promise unkept, a message undelivered, a task abandoned — and the person cannot move on to whatever comes after death until it is resolved.

A warning. The revenant returns to warn the living about something — a coming danger, a secret, a mistake that must be corrected.

Sheer malevolence. In darker tales, the revenant simply returns to cause harm, haunt, and terrorize, driven by bitterness, hatred, or some dark force.

The key point is: a revenant has intent. It is not wandering aimlessly. It came back for something.

In folklore, revenants were genuinely feared because they were thought to be dangerous to the living. They could reportedly spread disease, cause madness, bring misfortune to families, and physically harm people. Communities that believed in revenants often took drastic measures — digging up corpses and burning or dismembering them — to make sure a suspected revenant could not rise again.

A revenant does not simply drift and haunt. It acts. It pursues. It interacts with the physical world in ways a faint spirit cannot.
How It Differs from Similar Words

It is very easy to confuse "revenant" with other words in this space. Here is how to keep them straight:

A ghost is the general term for the spirit of someone who has died and lingers in some form. A revenant is a specific kind of ghost — one whose defining feature is the act of returning. All revenants are ghosts in a broad sense, but not all ghosts are revenants.

A zombie (in traditional Haitian folklore, not Hollywood movies) is a corpse reanimated under someone else's control — it is enslaved and mindless. A revenant acts on its own will and has its own motivations. A revenant is not controlled by anyone.

A vampire is a creature that feeds on blood. In some old European folklore, vampires were actually considered a type of revenant — a dead person who returned. But in modern usage, vampires are their own distinct category with their own rules. Most revenants are not vampires.

A specter or phantom is usually an apparition — something seen but not fully physically present. A revenant leans toward the physical and tangible side of the spectrum.

The word "revenant" appears most often today in literature, film, and storytelling — especially in the horror, fantasy, and gothic genres. When a writer uses the word "revenant" instead of just "ghost," they are deliberately signaling something specific: this being came back, and it came back on purpose.

The 2015 film The Revenant used the word in a slightly loose, metaphorical way — the main character does not literally die and return from the dead, but he survives something unsurvivable and claws his way back to life in order to seek revenge. The film borrows the word's spirit perfectly: a man who should be dead, who returned, who came back for a reason.

In fantasy games, books, and role-playing settings, "revenant" is used to describe a specific type of undead creature — one that retains memory, personality, and will, and is driven by a powerful purpose, usually revenge. This distinguishes it from mindless undead like skeletons and zombies.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Whenever you see or hear the word "revenant," think of three things:

Dead. Returned. Purposeful.

If a dead being simply lingers — it is a ghost. If a dead being comes back with presence, physicality, and intent — it is a revenant.

"The villagers whispered that old Maren had become a revenant — that she had crawled back from her grave, fury intact, to punish the man who had stolen her land."

That single sentence captures everything: she was dead, she returned, and she came back wanting something.
13834:
Revenge is the act of deliberately harming someone because they harmed you first. It is a response — specifically a harmful response — to something hurtful that was done to you. When you take revenge on someone, you are intentionally making them suffer, lose, or feel pain, because they made you suffer, lose, or feel pain.

The key idea is: you were hurt, so now you hurt them back.
The emotional heart of revenge

Revenge is never accidental or neutral. It is always driven by a powerful, burning emotional desire to "even the score." When someone harms you — insults you, betrays you, humiliates you, hurts someone you love, or takes something from you — it can create a deep sense of injustice and anger inside you. You feel that something unfair happened to you, and you want that person to feel what you felt. You want to restore a kind of emotional balance: they made me suffer, so I want them to suffer too.

This is the emotional engine of revenge. It is personal, it is intense, and it is directed at a specific person or group.
The three essential ingredients

For something to truly be called "revenge," three things must be present:

1. A prior harm or wrong.
Someone must have done something to hurt you first. Revenge is always a reaction. It does not come out of nowhere — there is always a triggering event, real or perceived, that the person seeking revenge believes was unjust or hurtful.

2. A deliberate intent to cause harm in return.
Revenge is never accidental. If you bump into someone who once hurt you and they happen to spill their coffee, that is not revenge. Revenge requires that you make a conscious choice to act, with the specific goal of making that person pay for what they did.

3. A personal motive — "because of what they did to me."
This is what separates revenge from other forms of action. The motivation is deeply personal. You are not acting on behalf of a system of law or society. You are acting for yourself, out of your own pain and anger, because you were the one wronged.
Revenge is personal, not official

This is one of the most important things to understand about the word. Revenge is something a person takes into their own hands. It is not the same as legal punishment or official justice.

If someone steals from you and a court sends them to prison, that is justice — a neutral, official system deciding on a consequence.

If you personally go and slash that person's tires, destroy their property, or harm them in some way because they stole from you, that is revenge — a private, personal act of retaliation driven by your own anger and pain.

Revenge bypasses courts, rules, and authorities. It is you deciding: I will be the one to make them pay.
Revenge does not have to be physical

A common misunderstanding is that revenge only means physical violence. In reality, revenge can take many forms:

  • Spreading damaging information about someone who betrayed you
  • Ruining someone's reputation after they ruined yours
  • Getting someone fired after they got you fired
  • Publicly humiliating someone who humiliated you
  • Stealing from someone who stole from you
  • Sabotaging someone's work, relationships, or plans

What all of these have in common is the deliberate intent to cause harm in return for a harm already received. The method does not matter — what defines revenge is the motive.
Revenge is not always proportional

Another important nuance: revenge does not have to be equal to the original harm. In fact, in many cases, it goes far beyond the original harm.

If someone teases you once, and you dedicate months to completely destroying their career in response — that is still revenge, just wildly disproportionate revenge. The desire for revenge can grow in a person's mind until it becomes something much larger than the original offense. This is why revenge can spiral into cycles: Person A hurts Person B → Person B takes revenge → Person A considers that disproportionate and takes further revenge → and so on. This is called a cycle of revenge or cycle of retaliation, and it can go on indefinitely, with each side feeling justified because the other "started it."
Revenge vs. similar words

Revenge vs. vengeance: These two words are very close in meaning and are often used interchangeably. "Vengeance" tends to feel slightly more intense and old-fashioned; "revenge" is the everyday word. Both mean the same fundamental thing.

Revenge vs. retaliation: Retaliation is a broader word that simply means "striking back." It is often used in military, political, or professional contexts and can be more calculated and less emotionally charged. Revenge is more personal and more emotionally driven.

Revenge vs. retribution: Retribution means punishment that is considered deserved or just — it has a moral flavor and is often used in legal or philosophical discussions. Revenge is messier and more personal; it does not need to be "fair" or "deserved" in any objective sense.

Revenge vs. payback: Payback is an informal, casual word for the same idea — "I'll get payback for this." It is less intense in tone than "revenge."
Common ways the word is used

You will almost always see "revenge" used with these verbs and phrases:

  • "get revenge on someone" — the most common phrasing: She got revenge on him for lying to her.
  • "take revenge on someone" — He took revenge on the people who had betrayed him.
  • "seek revenge" — to actively pursue it: After years of humiliation, she finally began seeking revenge.
  • "exact revenge" — a more formal/literary phrasing meaning to carry it out: He waited patiently, biding his time before exacting revenge.
  • "an act of revenge" — referring to a specific harmful action done out of revenge
  • "out of revenge" — explaining the motive: He did it out of revenge, not greed.
  • "in revenge for" — specifying what it was in response to: The attack was in revenge for what had happened the previous year.
  • "sweet revenge" — when revenge feels particularly satisfying: After everything they put her through, exposing their dishonesty felt like sweet revenge.
  • "a revenge plot" — a plan to get revenge
The psychology behind it: why people want revenge

Understanding why people want revenge deepens your understanding of the word itself.

When you are harmed, especially if it feels unfair or malicious, you experience a loss of control and a wound to your dignity or pride. Wanting revenge is partly a desire to restore a sense of power — to prove that you are not powerless, that actions against you have consequences, and that the person who hurt you will not simply "get away with it."

There is also a deep human sense of fairness at work. Most people feel instinctively that if someone causes suffering, they should experience suffering in return. This is why revenge can feel emotionally satisfying — in the moment of imagining it, or even carrying it out, it feels like balance has been restored.

However, many people who actually carry out revenge report that it does not give them the relief or satisfaction they expected. The emotional wound from the original harm often remains. This has given rise to the idea that revenge is ultimately hollow or self-defeating — that it perpetuates pain rather than ending it.
A famous saying about revenge

"Revenge is a dish best served cold."

This well-known expression means that revenge is most satisfying — and most effective — when it is not carried out immediately in the heat of anger, but after a long period of careful, patient waiting and planning. The "cold" refers to the passage of time, and implies that a cold, calculating approach to revenge is more powerful than a hot, impulsive reaction.
Summary

Revenge is the deliberate act of harming someone because they harmed you first. It is personal, emotionally driven, and always reactive — it comes in response to a perceived wrong. It is not official punishment or neutral justice; it is you choosing to make someone pay, in your own way, for what they did to you. It can range from mild acts to extreme ones, can be proportional or wildly disproportionate, and is fueled by feelings of anger, pain, and the deep human desire to restore a sense of fairness and power after being wronged.
13835:
Revenue is the total amount of money that flows into a person, business, or organization from their normal activities — counted before any expenses or costs are subtracted.

Think of it as the full pile of money you receive. What you do with that pile afterward — paying rent, salaries, bills — doesn't change the revenue figure. Revenue is purely about what came in.
A Simple Example to Ground This

Imagine you run a small lemonade stall. Over the course of a Saturday, you sell 100 cups at ₹10 each. The total money you collect — ₹1,000 — is your revenue.

Now, you spent ₹300 on lemons, sugar, and cups. That ₹300 is your expense. After subtracting it, you're left with ₹700 — that's your profit.

Notice: revenue is the ₹1,000 — the entire amount that came in. Not ₹700. Revenue doesn't care about your costs. It's simply the total money received from doing what you do.

For a business:
A company's revenue comes from selling its products or services. A shoe company earns revenue when customers buy shoes. A software company earns revenue when customers pay for subscriptions. A hotel earns revenue when guests pay for rooms. All of this counts as revenue regardless of how much the company spends to produce or deliver those things.

For a government:
Governments earn revenue primarily through taxes — income tax, sales tax, import duties, and fees. When citizens and businesses pay taxes, that money becomes the government's revenue, which it then uses to fund roads, hospitals, schools, and so on. This is why you'll often hear phrases like "government revenue" or "tax revenue" in news about national budgets.

For an individual (less common but valid):
If you rent out a room in your house for ₹8,000 a month, that ₹8,000 is your rental revenue. If you also do freelance design work and earn ₹15,000 from it, your total revenue from both activities is ₹23,000. Here, revenue simply means all the money you've received.
The Most Important Distinction: Revenue vs. Profit

This is where most learners get confused, so it's worth being very precise.

Revenue = Total money received (before any deductions).
Profit = Money left over after all expenses have been subtracted from revenue.

A company can have enormous revenue and still be losing money — if its expenses are even higher. For example, a startup might earn ₹50 crore in revenue but spend ₹70 crore running the business. Its revenue is ₹50 crore, but it has a loss of ₹20 crore, not a profit.

This is why investors, analysts, and business owners track both revenue and profit separately — revenue tells you how much is coming in; profit tells you whether the business is actually sustainable.
Revenue vs. Income — A Nuance Worth Knowing

In everyday speech, people sometimes use "revenue" and "income" interchangeably, and that's acceptable in casual conversation. But in formal business and accounting language, there's often a distinction:

  • Revenue almost always refers to the top-line total — the gross amount received before anything is taken out.
  • Income (especially "net income") often refers to what remains after expenses have been deducted — essentially, profit.

You'll sometimes hear businesspeople refer to revenue as the "top line" of a financial statement because it appears at the very top, before all the deductions are listed below it. Profit, sitting at the bottom after all subtractions, is called the "bottom line." When someone says "it affects our bottom line," they mean it affects their profit.
Two Kinds of Revenue a Business Can Have

1. Operating revenue — money earned from the company's main activity. For a bakery, this is money from selling bread and cakes. For an airline, it's ticket sales. This is the core, recurring source of revenue that the business was built around.

2. Non-operating revenue — money earned from secondary or incidental activities, not the core business. For example, if that same bakery keeps some money in a savings account and earns interest on it, that interest is non-operating revenue. If a company owns a building and rents out part of it, the rent is non-operating revenue. It's still revenue, but it doesn't come from the company's main purpose.

This distinction matters because operating revenue tells you how healthy the actual business is, while non-operating revenue can be unpredictable or one-time.
How the Word Is Used in Real Life

You'll encounter "revenue" constantly in news, business, and finance. Here are the kinds of sentences where it appears naturally:

  • "The company reported revenue of $5 billion this quarter." — meaning it received $5 billion from its sales activities.
  • "Revenue fell by 12% due to lower consumer demand." — the total money coming in decreased.
  • "The government is looking for new sources of revenue." — ways to bring in more money (new taxes, fees, etc.).
  • "Revenue growth was strong, but the company still posted a loss." — more money came in than before, but expenses were even higher.
  • "Advertising revenue accounts for 80% of the platform's earnings." — most of its incoming money comes from advertisers.
The One-Sentence Definition You Can Always Rely On

Revenue is the total money received by a business, government, or individual from their activities or operations, measured before any expenses or costs are deducted.

Everything else — profit, net income, earnings — comes after you've done something with that revenue. Revenue itself is simply the starting point: the full amount that walked through the door.
13836: To reverberate means to bounce back and keep spreading, whether that's a sound echoing through a space, or the effects of an event continuing to be felt long after it happened.

Picture yourself inside a large, empty cave. You shout. What happens? Your voice doesn't just go forward and die. It hits the rocky walls, bounces back, hits another wall, bounces again — and you keep hearing it, layered and fading, for several seconds. That is reverberation. The sound is traveling back and forth, filling the space, before it slowly fades away.

This is the original, core meaning of reverberate: a sound bounces off surfaces and keeps going, filling a space with echoes.

The thunder reverberated through the valley.
Her singing voice reverberated beautifully inside the stone church.
The gunshot reverberated off the warehouse walls.

Notice the pattern: there is a source (thunder, a voice, a gunshot), a space (valley, church, warehouse), and the sound keeps bouncing and filling that space rather than stopping instantly.
The Key Feeling of the Word

Before we go further, here are three qualities that "reverberate" almost always carries, no matter how you use it:

1. It keeps going. It doesn't stop at once. It echoes, ripples, and lingers.

2. It spreads outward. It reaches places beyond where it started.

3. It has power. You almost never use "reverberate" for something tiny or weak. The word carries weight. It suggests that something was strong enough to travel and persist.

Keep these three qualities in your mind — they are the soul of this word.
The Figurative Meaning: Events and Effects

This is where the word becomes truly powerful and is most commonly used. Just like sound bounces off walls and keeps spreading, the effects of an important event can bounce through society, through people's lives, and through time — continuing to affect things long after the original event is over.

When we say something reverberates, we mean: its consequences, shock, or influence spread widely and are felt for a long time.

The 2008 financial crisis reverberated around the world for years.

The crisis happened. But its effects — job losses, collapsed businesses, broken families, changed policies — kept spreading and bouncing across the globe, affecting millions of people long after the initial crash. That spreading, lingering impact is the reverberation.

His resignation reverberated throughout the entire company.

He left one day. But the shock, the uncertainty, the changes in roles and leadership — those effects rippled through every department, every employee, for months.

Her words reverberated in his mind long after she had left the room.

She spoke her words once. But he kept hearing them in his head, being affected by them again and again. The words "bounced" inside him, just like sound bouncing off walls.

The assassination of the archduke reverberated across the whole of Europe.

One event. But its shockwaves spread far and wide, touching every nation — just like a shout filling a huge cave.
A Closer Look at the Figurative Use

Notice what "reverberate" adds that a simple word like "affect" or "impact" does not. Compare:

  • The decision affected the company. — Fine. Neutral. Simple.
  • The decision reverberated throughout the company. — Now you feel it. The decision sent shockwaves. It kept rippling through every corner. People are still feeling it.

"Reverberate" doesn't just say something happened. It says: something happened, and its effects spread and kept spreading, touching many things, and didn't stop quickly. It gives a sense of scale and duration.

"Reverberate" is a strong, expressive word. Writers and speakers use it when they want to show that something was significant enough to send ripples far and wide.

You would not say:

❌ Her small comment about the weather reverberated across the office.

Unless that comment somehow caused a big, lasting reaction, this would feel exaggerated. The word naturally pairs with things that have real weight — historical events, powerful speeches, major decisions, tragedies, shocking news.

You would say:

✅ The prime minister's speech reverberated across the nation.
✅ The explosion reverberated through the building.
✅ The scandal reverberated for decades.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Echo — Close in meaning, but echo is simpler. It usually means one reflected copy of a sound, or a direct repetition. Reverberate implies multiple bounces, a richer, more sustained spreading.

Resound — Means to fill a place with sound, or to be famous/celebrated. ("His name resounded throughout history.") It's about fullness and fame, not necessarily the bouncing and lingering that reverberate emphasizes.

Ripple — Often used figuratively like reverberate, but ripple is gentler. Ripples are small, soft waves. Reverberations are more powerful — they come from something loud or forceful.

Ring out — Describes a sound being heard clearly and loudly, but it doesn't carry the idea of ongoing bouncing and spreading the way reverberate does.
The Mental Image to Lock It In Forever

Think of a large bell being struck.

The moment it is hit, a deep, rich sound booms outward. But it doesn't stop — the sound rings and rings, gradually fading, filling the air around it for a long time. You feel it in your chest. It travels. It lingers.

That is reverberate. Whether it's sound bouncing off walls, or the effects of a great event bouncing through time and society — the image is always the same: something powerful, spreading outward, bouncing and persisting, slow to fade.

LiteralA sound bounces off surfaces and fills a space with echoes
FigurativeThe effects of an event spread widely and continue to be felt for a long time
Key qualitiesPersistence · Spread · Power
ToneStrong, expressive — used for significant things

Once you see a word like reverberate in a sentence, ask yourself: what is bouncing, what is it bouncing through, and how long does it last? Answer those three things, and you have fully understood the word in its context.
13837:
Imagine you're inside a large, empty hall. You clap your hands once. But instead of the sound ending cleanly and immediately, you hear it linger — it seems to fill the room, bouncing around and fading slowly. That sustained, lingering quality of the sound is called reverberation.

In its most fundamental sense, reverberation is the persistence of sound in a space after the original source of that sound has stopped, caused by sound waves bouncing repeatedly off surfaces.

When a sound is produced, it doesn't travel in just one direction. It spreads outward in all directions like a ripple in water. These sound waves hit the walls, ceiling, floor, and objects in a room, and they bounce back. Then they bounce again. And again. Each bounce sends the sound back toward you, slightly weaker each time, until the energy is fully absorbed and the sound finally dies out.

Your ears receive not just the original sound, but also dozens — sometimes hundreds — of these reflected copies of it, all arriving at slightly different times and from different directions. Because these reflections arrive so rapidly and blend together so seamlessly, you don't hear them as separate sounds. Instead, you experience them as one continuous, rich, fading sound. That blended, fading afterlife of a sound is the reverberation.

A key point: reverberation is not a single bounce. It is the combined effect of many, many reflections happening almost simultaneously.
Reverberation vs. Echo — Know the Difference

This is one of the most important distinctions to understand, because people often confuse the two.

  • An echo is a clearly distinct repetition of a sound that you hear as a separate event. If you shout across a canyon, you hear your voice come back to you as a recognisable, separate copy of what you said — that's an echo. It requires enough distance between you and the reflecting surface so that the return trip of the sound takes a noticeable amount of time (at least about 1/10th of a second).
  • Reverberation, on the other hand, happens when the reflecting surfaces are much closer, so the reflected sound waves arrive back at your ears too quickly to be heard as separate events. They pile on top of one another and merge into a single, sustained, gradually fading sound.

Simple way to remember it: An echo sounds like your voice coming back to you. Reverberation sounds like your voice staying around you.
Where You Encounter Reverberation in Real Life

Reverberation is everywhere, once you know to listen for it:

  • In a cathedral or large church: When the choir sings or the organ plays, the music doesn't stop the instant the musicians stop. It hangs in the air, swelling and slowly dissolving. That is reverberation — and in many ways, it is what gives such spaces their awe-inspiring, grand quality.
  • In a tiled bathroom: Have you noticed that your voice sounds richer and fuller when you sing in the shower or bathroom? Hard tiles reflect sound very efficiently and create strong reverberation.
  • In an empty room vs. a furnished room: An empty room with bare walls feels "echoey" because sound bounces freely. A room full of furniture, carpets, and curtains sounds "dead" or "dry" because soft materials absorb sound waves instead of reflecting them, reducing reverberation.
  • In music production and recording: Sound engineers deliberately add reverberation to recorded music to give it warmth, depth, and a sense of space. Without any reverberation, a recording can sound flat and lifeless. This is why "reverb" is one of the most commonly used effects in music.
  • In a concert hall: Acoustic engineers carefully design concert halls to produce the right amount of reverberation — enough to make the music sound rich and full, but not so much that it becomes muddy and unclear.

Like many words rooted in physical experience, reverberation has a powerful figurative use — and this is just as common as the literal one.

Figuratively, reverberations are the continuing effects, consequences, or influences of an event that keep being felt long after the event itself has ended — just as sound keeps being heard after the source has gone silent.

Examples:

  • "The reverberations of the financial crash were felt for decades." — The effects of the crash didn't end when the crash did. They kept rippling through society, economies, and lives for a long time afterward.
  • "His speech sent reverberations through the entire political landscape." — His words didn't just affect the moment; they triggered ongoing reactions, shifts, and responses that spread far and wide.
  • "The reverberations of the scandal damaged the company's reputation for years." — The impact kept echoing through time, long after the original incident.

In this figurative sense, reverberation captures the idea that significant events — like significant sounds — do not simply stop when they are over. They echo onward.

The word is very commonly used in its plural form, reverberations, especially in the figurative sense. This is because consequences and ripple effects are rarely just one thing — they spread in many directions, affecting many people and situations. When you say "the reverberations of the war," you are acknowledging that there were many different, ongoing effects spreading in many directions, just as a sound in a room creates many different reflections bouncing in many directions.

One nuance worth knowing: reverberation can vary enormously in duration and intensity, and both matter.

  • Short reverberation (a fraction of a second): Sounds clean and intimate. Think of a small, carpeted office.
  • Long reverberation (several seconds): Sounds grand, spacious, even overwhelming. Think of a stone cathedral.
  • Too much reverberation: Can make speech impossible to understand, because each word bleeds into the next before you've had time to process it.
  • Too little reverberation: Can make a space feel sterile and cold.

This spectrum matters because when people use "reverberations" figuratively, the implied intensity and duration of the effects also varies — small reverberations fade quickly; profound reverberations reshape everything around them and last a very long time.

Literal: Reverberation is the way sound lingers and fades in a space because its waves keep bouncing off surfaces after the source has stopped making noise.

Figurative: Reverberation is the way the impact of an event keeps spreading and being felt long after the event itself is over.

To revere someone or something means to feel a very deep, almost sacred level of respect and admiration for them — so deep that it borders on awe or worship.

It is not ordinary respect. When you revere something, you place it on the highest pedestal possible in your mind. You see it as extraordinarily great, precious, or noble. You treat it with the utmost care and honour. There is a sense of humility in it too — you feel small in comparison to what you revere.

Think of it this way: you might like your neighbour. You might respect your boss. You might admire a talented athlete. But you revere a figure who feels almost beyond ordinary human greatness to you — someone like a spiritual leader, a national hero, or a beloved ancestor whose wisdom seems timeless.

Revering something involves three layers happening at once:

Deep admiration — You genuinely believe the person or thing is extraordinary, not just good.

A sense of awe — There is something almost overwhelming about the greatness you see. It moves you emotionally.

A sacred quality — You treat the subject as if it should not be taken lightly, criticised carelessly, or treated as ordinary. It feels almost untouchable.

This is why the word is often used in religious or spiritual contexts, but it does not have to be. You can revere a person, a place, an idea, a text, or a tradition — anything that holds the highest possible worth in someone's eyes.

• "People all over the world revere Mahatma Gandhi for his courage and his peaceful fight for justice."
  • "The villagers revere the old temple; they believe it is sacred ground."
  • "She revered her grandmother — to her, the old woman's wisdom was priceless."
  • "In that country, the founding document of the nation is revered as something almost holy."
  • "The students revered their professor, hanging on every word he said."

Notice in all these examples, the feeling is not casual. It is intense, deep, and lasting.
How It Compares to Similar Words

This is important for a learner, because "revere" is often confused with weaker words.

Respect is everyday and neutral. You can respect someone you've just met. Revere is far stronger.

Admire means you appreciate someone's qualities — perhaps their skill, looks, or talent. It is a positive feeling, but it is lighter. You can admire a stranger's painting. You revere something that feels almost sacred to you.

Look up to is a casual phrase that means you see someone as a role model. Revering goes deeper — it carries awe and a near-devotional quality.

Worship is the closest word to revere, but worship is usually reserved for a god or deity. Revere can be used for people, places, and ideas without implying actual religious worship. Think of revere as a slightly more restrained, more broadly usable version of worship.

Venerate is almost a perfect synonym for revere. Both mean the same thing. However, venerate is even more formal and is used slightly more in religious or ceremonial language.
Who or What Is Typically Revered?

This word is usually used for:

  • Historical or national heroes (e.g., founding figures of a country)
  • Religious or spiritual figures (e.g., prophets, saints, monks)
  • Beloved elders or ancestors whose wisdom is treasured
  • Sacred places (e.g., temples, mountains, ancient sites)
  • Sacred texts or traditions
  • Great artists, thinkers, or leaders who shaped history

It would sound strange to say "I revere this sandwich" or "I revere my new phone." The word demands a subject of significant moral, spiritual, or historical weight.
What Revering Looks Like in Behaviour

Because revere is a verb describing a feeling, you might wonder: how does someone show that they revere something? They:

  • Speak about the subject with care and reverence, never mockingly
  • Defend it if others disrespect it
  • Study it deeply or preserve it
  • Approach it with humility — they do not assume they are equal to it
  • Often pass on their admiration to others (children, students, followers)

It does not mean simply liking something. You like ice cream. You revere a hero.

It does not mean being a fan. A fan's admiration can be shallow or trend-based. Revering is deep, serious, and lasting.

It does not mean obeying. You can revere someone without following their orders — a person might revere a deceased philosopher they never met.

Though you didn't ask for etymology, you will encounter these related words in your reading, so knowing them is part of understanding "revere" fully:

  • Reverence (noun) — the feeling or attitude of revering. "She spoke of her mentor with great reverence."
  • Revered (adjective) — describes a person or thing that is widely revered. "He was a revered leader."
  • Reverent (adjective) — describes a person who is showing reverence, or a tone/atmosphere that feels deeply respectful. "They stood in reverent silence before the monument."
  • Reverently (adverb) — done in a reverent way. "She reverently placed the old photograph back in its frame."
  • Irreverent (adjective) — the opposite. Describes someone who treats serious or sacred things with disrespect or casual humor. "His irreverent jokes about the ceremony made people uncomfortable."
If you ever need to recall this word quickly: to revere = to hold in the deepest possible respect and awe, treating something as almost sacred.
13839:
When someone or something is described as revered, it means they are held in the deepest, most profound respect — a respect so strong that it borders on worship or devotion. It goes far beyond ordinary admiration. People don't just think highly of a revered person; they treat them with a kind of honor that feels almost sacred.

Think of it as respect turned all the way up to its highest possible level.
How it differs from ordinary respect

Everyday respect is something you might feel for a good manager, a kind neighbor, or a skilled colleague. That respect is real, but it's ordinary.

Revered is something else entirely. When someone is revered:

  • Their name is spoken with a certain weight and seriousness
  • Their words are treated as precious and not easily dismissed
  • People feel a sense of awe in their presence or even just thinking about them
  • Their legacy or memory is carefully protected and honored
  • There is often an emotional quality to the respect — something warm, devoted, and heartfelt

If respect is a candle, being revered is a bonfire.
Who or what can be revered?

The word is used for people, places, objects, and even ideas — but only when they carry significant weight and meaning.

People most commonly described as revered:

  • Spiritual or religious leaders (a revered saint, a revered guru)
  • Elders and ancestors in a community
  • Great historical figures who shaped a nation or culture
  • Scientists, philosophers, or artists whose work has had a lasting, profound impact
  • Teachers or mentors who have transformed people's lives

Places and things described as revered:

  • Ancient temples, holy sites, sacred rivers — places that communities treat with deep devotion
  • A nation's flag or constitution — symbols that carry enormous emotional and moral weight
  • Old traditions or texts that a community holds as precious

The key rule: Something is revered when a group of people — a community, a nation, a generation, a religion — collectively decides that it deserves the highest honor. It is almost always tied to a larger sense of meaning, history, or virtue.

This is what makes the word special. When you respect someone, it can be a cool, rational judgment: "This person is competent and trustworthy." That's good, but it stays in the head.

When you revere someone, it moves into the heart. There's awe. There's gratitude. There's a feeling that this person (or place, or thing) represents something larger than themselves — a set of values, a sacrifice, a kind of wisdom that most people can only aspire to.

Imagine how people speak about Nelson Mandela, Mahatma Gandhi, or a beloved grandmother who held a family together through hardship for decades. The tone changes. The voice softens or deepens. There's a seriousness and warmth. That feeling — and the status it reflects — is what "revered" captures.

"Dr. Abdul Kalam is a revered figure in India."

This means people don't just admire Kalam — they hold him in the deepest honor. His memory is almost sacred to many, treated with great care and devotion.

"The old temple is revered by the villagers, who have maintained it for centuries."

The villagers don't just find the temple interesting or historic. They treat it as deeply holy and precious — with a devotion that goes beyond ordinary appreciation.

"She was a revered teacher whose lessons her students carried throughout their lives."

Her students didn't just like her. They held her in a kind of deep, lasting gratitude and honor — the way you might honor someone who shaped who you are.

"The revered constitution of that country has stood for over two hundred years."

The citizens view their constitution not just as a useful legal document, but as something almost sacred — a foundation to be honored and protected.

It's worth being clear about what the word doesn't carry:

  • It does not mean feared. A revered person is admired with love and honor, not intimidated by. (Though in rare cases, a figure can be both feared and revered at once — such as a strict but deeply wise elder — but the words mean different things.)
  • It does not mean famous or popular. A celebrity can be wildly popular without being revered. Revered implies depth — a kind of respect built on genuine virtue, wisdom, sacrifice, or meaning — not just fame or entertainment value.
  • It does not mean perfect. Revered people can have flaws. The word reflects how others perceive and honor them, not a claim that they were flawless.
  • It is not casual. You would not use "revered" for small, everyday things. You would not say "This coffee shop is revered by the neighborhood" (that would sound odd and exaggerated). The word is reserved for things that carry real, lasting, and deep significance.

You'll most often see or hear "revered" in:

  • Writing about historical or religious figures
  • Discussions about culture, tradition, or heritage
  • Descriptions of important places or symbols
  • Tributes to great teachers, mentors, or leaders
  • Literature and journalism where formal, elevated language is used

It is a formal word. It carries weight. When a writer chooses to call something "revered," they are signaling: "This is not ordinary. This deserves your deepest respect."
A one-sentence summary to anchor it all

Revered means held in the deepest, most profound, and heartfelt respect — the kind of honor that feels almost sacred, and that entire communities share together for a person, place, or thing of exceptional significance.
